placements.section: Attention names answer different questions
placements.purpose: Read the boxes as different questions about one model. A causal, multi-head layer can still use scaled dot-product scoring: the choices combine. The first two boxes guide this foundations route; the head/KV box leads to the separate Attention Heads route. Our table below spells out these questions without assuming that every research method fits only one box.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Follow the input into recurrent state
placements.purpose: Follow the two incoming arrows before the outgoing one: one carries the previous summary and the other carries the current token representation. Reusing this cell creates a chain of computed states. The source picture labels one four-word step; our formula and three-token probe below describe the same dependency with different inputs.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Follow the summary into output tokens
placements.purpose: Trace the single middle arrow: all source information available to this decoder crosses the same context-vector handoff. The left and right chains can have different numbers of steps, as the English and French examples show. The next-token vocabulary prediction belongs on the decoder side; the context vector is an input representation, not a distribution over words.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Quantify one possible fading effect
placements.purpose: The changing color illustrates a possible loss of earlier contributions as the summary is updated. Treat that as motivation for a test, rather than a guarantee that every recurrent model erases its first words. The scalar calculation below specifies one retention factor and measures its exact effect.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: A context vector for each output step
placements.purpose: Each source state contributes its entire feature vector, multiplied by one scalar weight. The colored proportions describe contributions to one returned context, rather than probabilities that the decoder has already emitted those words. These are the source presentation’s four states; the worked calculation later uses our three retained rows.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: A complete small calculation
placements.purpose: Read the middle path first: compare the available query with every state, normalize the scores, and combine those states. Only afterward does the output-side computation use the context to score vocabulary entries. The source uses four English positions and rounded displayed values; our calculation below independently checks three states and keeps source-position weights separate from vocabulary probabilities.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Read an alignment matrix correctly
placements.purpose: Follow a row to see which source positions contribute to that output step; follow successive rows to see the retrieval change. The stronger cells need not form a diagonal when translation changes word order. This is a source illustration of alignment, not a learned result from our project or a requirement that attention always produces one-to-one matches.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Why the score is called additive
placements.purpose: The two branches first project the decoder query and one source state to compatible widths. Their addition happens inside the scoring network, before tanh and the final scalar projection. It is separate from the weighted sum of values that happens after normalization.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Direction and magnitude both affect a dot product
placements.purpose: The three panels isolate the sign contributed by direction: aligned vectors can give a positive score, perpendicular vectors give zero, and opposite vectors can give a negative score. Length also matters through the product of the norms. Use the same-direction, different-length counterexample below to avoid reading this picture as a cosine-only comparison.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Why divide by a square root?
placements.purpose: The plotted scale is a typical score magnitude, approximately the square root of the width under the stated random-coordinate assumptions. It is not a plot of variance: the variance calculation below gives d before scaling. Learned or correlated coordinates need not follow this sketch.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Softmax derivatives explain the concern more precisely
placements.purpose: The second panel multiplies the scores, enlarging their differences and concentrating the weights. A common offset alone would leave the distribution unchanged. The source caption compresses the gradient consequence: the derivation below concerns the softmax Jacobian, and does not imply that every gradient in a model disappears.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Compute all three queries
placements.purpose: The source diagram contrasts output-step queries against input memory with queries and keys drawn from one sequence. The square shape follows from using the same number of query and source positions. It does not mean the normalized matrix must be symmetric, or that its diagonal is the only useful information.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: What happens when inputs change?
placements.purpose: Each arrow into the returned vector carries a source vector scaled by its attention weight. A changed input can change both the available content and the weights used to retrieve it. The six-word source illustration gives the structural picture; our numerical outputs above use the explicitly declared three-row fixture.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Shape and normalization are part of the meaning
placements.purpose: Read a row as one query choosing among the source columns. This source picture uses six tokens and rounded weights; our preceding matrix uses three synthetic rows. In both cases, normalization runs across source positions, and each output feature receives its mixture from that same query row.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Name the roles after their jobs
placements.purpose: Start at one token representation and follow its three branches. The query branch determines how that position asks, the key branch determines how a source can match, and the value branch determines the content delivered after matching. These are learned roles; the labels do not assign fixed linguistic meanings to coordinates.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Project the same three rows
placements.purpose: The three products create Q, K and V before any query–key score is normalized. The source diagram uses a five-token input with its own parameter values. Below, we apply the same three-branch operation to our three rows and named matrices, so every resulting number can be checked independently.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Follow the last query all the way through
placements.purpose: Follow Q and K into the score matrix, then follow V around the comparison branch into the final value mixture. This bypass explains why changing a value projection can change delivered features without changing the attention weights. The matrix axes and widths below give the exact contract for our smaller worked example.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Locate the target before drawing the triangle
placements.purpose: Use a row as the position making a prediction and a column as a possible source. The visible prefix grows one position at a time; entries strictly to the right are forbidden. The diagonal is allowed because that row predicts the following token from the current token and its prefix, as the shifted targets below make explicit.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Apply visibility before normalization
placements.purpose: The blocked entries contribute zero after exponentiation, so the denominator includes only allowed sources. The order is essential to the direct masked-softmax calculation. A row with no allowed finite score still needs explicit handling; the picture does not define a valid distribution for that case.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: Dropout changes a sample, not the intended mean
placements.purpose: The two outcomes illustrate the expectation calculation: a contribution sometimes becomes zero, and the survivors are enlarged by the reciprocal keep probability. Each sampled attention row need not sum to one. Our example below enumerates every keep/drop pattern and checks the immediate weighted mixture rather than claiming equality for a whole nonlinear model.

figures.capture: Chrome screenshot of the unmodified rendered figure region at 1920×1080 viewport; slide prose and browser controls outside the crop

placements.section: The same causal calculation in C++
placements.purpose: Read the stages in order and locate the mask between the scores and softmax. Dropout, when enabled for training, acts on normalized weights before the value mixture. The final arrow abbreviates multiplying the weights by V; the weight matrix itself is not the output Z. The C++ reference below checks the deterministic masked calculation without adding a dropout implementation; the earlier Python reference separately checks the dropout expectation.
